stemMd:
A study found that hospitals which publish their surgical outcomes online have lower post-operative mortality than hospitals which do not. The researchers concluded that publishing outcomes leads surgeons to take more care.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the researchers' conclusion?

options.label: A
options.textMd: Within the same hospitals, mortality fell after they began publishing outcomes, while in comparable hospitals that did not publish it stayed level.

options.label: B
options.textMd: Hospitals that publish outcomes tend to be larger and better funded than hospitals that do not.

options.label: C
options.textMd: Surgeons at hospitals that publish outcomes are, on average, more experienced than surgeons elsewhere.

options.label: D
options.textMd: Publishing outcomes online costs hospitals very little.

options.label: E
options.textMd: Some hospitals that publish outcomes still have high mortality rates.

explanationMd:
The evidence is a comparison between two different groups of hospitals, so the obvious objection is that they differed in other ways before anyone published anything. A strengthener should rule that out.

A before-and-after change inside the same hospitals, set against comparable hospitals that did not publish, does exactly that. The hospitals are compared with themselves, so fixed differences such as size or staff cannot explain the change, and the comparison group shows the fall was not a general trend.

**How to check.** Size and funding, and surgeon experience, are rival explanations for the mortality gap: they weaken the conclusion. A few publishing hospitals with high mortality is consistent with either view and changes little. The cost of publishing tells us nothing about its effect on surgeons.

distractorRationale.b: This offers a rival explanation: larger, better-funded hospitals might have lower mortality for reasons unrelated to publishing. It weakens the conclusion.
distractorRationale.c: More experienced surgeons are another reason for lower mortality that has nothing to do with publishing. This weakens the conclusion.
distractorRationale.e: The study compares averages. A few exceptions do not show that publishing has no effect, nor that it has one; the conclusion is essentially unchanged.
distractorRationale.d: Cost bears on whether publishing is worth doing, not on whether it changes surgeons' behaviour. It neither strengthens nor weakens the causal claim.

accessibilityText: An argument-analysis question. Hospitals that publish surgical outcomes online have lower post-operative mortality than those that do not, and researchers concluded publishing makes surgeons take more care. The question asks which statement most strengthens the conclusion. The options are: within the same hospitals mortality fell after they began publishing while comparable non-publishing hospitals stayed level; publishing hospitals are larger and better funded; their surgeons are more experienced; some publishing hospitals still have high mortality; publishing costs little.

provenance.notes: Original strengthen item. The key is a within-unit comparison with a control group; two distractors are rival causes that weaken, two are irrelevant.

review.author: bocconi-graduate-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: A provides within-hospital before/after evidence with a comparable control group, ruling out pre-existing differences between publishers and non-publishers, so it best supports publishing -> care. B and C offer alternative explanations (weaken). D is irrelevant to the causal mechanism. E is compatible with either view and does not strengthen.

review.notes: Author checked that exactly one option is defensible. Awaiting blind independent solve. Options were reordered after review to remove answer-position bias; ids and labels were remapped with the key.
